Modules: AI Security
Title: Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)
Context: The bank can see an attack happening, but the only person it can ban is Ezra
Full Text:
AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action?

“Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits.

Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries. An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it.

This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents").

This post rests on one principle:

The Intermediation Principle: The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation.

A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign.

The intermediary problem

Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. She runs their errands: groceries, appointments, paperwork, and flights. Ezra blends into the crowd.

The corner grocer used to know Amy. He knew what she bought and set aside what he thought she'd like. Now only Ezra comes in, carrying orders for four people, and the grocer can't tell whose preferences are whose. He doesn't want to turn Ezra away, because she brings him a lot of business.

Then Bob asks Ezra to buy him an iPhone. A week later he calls the store, says he never authorized the charge, and keeps the phone. To win the dispute, the store has to prove Bob asked for it. But the only person the store ever saw was Ezra.

Then Charlie gives Ezra a list of passwords: "I forgot mine, but it's one of these." Ezra patiently tries each one at Charlie's bank. The bank can see an attack happening, but the only person it can ban is Ezra. Banning Ezra also bans Amy, Bob, and Debra.

None of these business owners has a problem with Ezra herself. Their problem is that they can only see Ezra, not the person she's acting for. Swap Ezra for an AI Agent and the businesses for websites, and you have the web today.

A website owner wants sufficient visibility both to prevent bad behavior and to effectively monetize or get value from their Site. But as with Ezra, much of that visibility goes away with AI Agents. Below is a list of actions that a website owner might want to address that were previously solved, but are made more challenging by allowing Agents.

In nearly every challenge above, the Site bears the primary cost. That outcome follows from how trust works when an intermediary is involved.

Our vision

Our aim is an Internet where all Users have equal or greater access to websites than they had before. Before Agents, a Site was typically able to mitigate these risks with a collection of techniques, including fingerprinting the User’s device, session, and history. Users could still browse using private browsing mode, and we believe Agents should be able to do that as well. But they probably won’t be able to log in to a bank without additional verification.

None of this requires an Agent to act like a human or a human to be present for every action. It requires that Sites have the means to obtain or require information about the User to hold them accountable, when applicable, with or without an Agent.

What people have tried, and why they fall short

A common proposal is for Agents to pass a Site's CAPTCHA through to the User to solve. That proves some human is present at that moment (“human in the loop”, or HITL), and nothing more. HITL is primarily a mechanism to prevent mistakes from misalignment. Misalignment is an issue between the Operator and the User, and resolving it does not resolve the majority of the problems above. For example, it can't tell Bob from anyone else (Traffic commingling), and it says nothing about who the Agent acts for the rest of the time. Additionally, Agents exist to remove friction, and HITL adds back that friction, so Operators are incentivized to remove or bypass it for the User.

Another common proposal is to use tightly scoped access controls. Agents are built to do anything a User could, so in practice they ask for, and get, permission to do everything. A scope of "everything" tells the Site nothing. And even a narrow scope only says what the Agent was allowed to do. It doesn't say who answers when the Agent gets it wrong, which is the question the Site actually needs answered.

What the web needs

The web needs tools and protocols that allow Sites and Agents to collaborate to determine what behaviors and actions are allowed, as well as express preferences and policies from Sites to Agents, all in a way that can be reasonably supported by all Sites and Agents. Fortunately, work is already underway along all of these fronts, and many, if not all, of these can be addressed by applying existing standards.

Protocols

Agents and Sites can engage in explicit protocols for solving some of the problems above. For instance, MOLE is one upcoming approach that aims for rate limiting without User-specific identifiers, allowing Sites to transition away from implicit identities and towards explicit protocols for accomplishing the same goal. This is similar to the x402 protocol, which aims to enable payments on the web while remaining privacy-preserving. We are actively exploring ways in which we can leverage existing protocols for addressing other problems, as well as exploring designing new protocols when existing solutions fall short.

Identities

When discussing Agent Identity, Web Bot Auth (WBA) is our preferred method. WBA allows an Agent to sign its requests, which provides a secure way for an Agent to identify itself (and, implicitly, the Operator). We must still define a mechanism that supports multiple intermediaries: when Agent A uses Agent B inside Browser C, the Site needs to be able to know this, so that the Site can correctly ensure that access by Agent A is correctly understood and controlled, for example, in order to prevent Policy circumvention.

Other types of identifying information, such as session, account, or even User-specific IDs, might be necessary, depending on the context. We are working with the relevant standards to explore ways to communicate such identifying information.

Let’s take a look into types of Identity in regards to a User. Ultimately, Identity is a spectrum that trades various degrees of information about a user, while ideally practicing principles of data minimization. Identity provides us a mechanism to answer “who are you?” in pursuit of answering the follow-up questions of: “are you who you say you are?” and “can we trust you?”.

In many cases, identifying information isn’t needed, and privacy-preserving methods for moderating access to agents, such as through Privacy Pass and MOLE, can help us answer “can we trust you?” without needing to answer “who are you?”. Private Access Tokens was one early way in which we tried to establish trust without identifying the user, and MOLE is intended to be the successor to this technology However, there are cases where graduated forms of disclosure along this spectrum would be needed, and you can generally characterize them in the following ways:

Nothing - Users may act on the internet while bringing no identifiers to the table.

Session - Sites require some way of linking requests in the same session to a single agent. This allows the Site to establish reputation for a given session and act on it accordingly. For example, Poppy has a notion of a session ID for exactly this purpose.

Account - Sites require a way of attributing requests to the same User across sessions. This might be a stable identifier assigned by an Operator or third party to a User that persists across the account with the Operator, such as a single Agent visiting the same Site every day using the same identifier. An example use case this would enable is: “Bind your Site account to your Agent account”.

Unique - Some Sites might require a unique, per-User identifier provisioned by a third party that persists across Operators, accounts, Agents, and sessions. This may be useful for high risk actions, or for Sites that need to provide limited access to an expensive resource or that have very restrictive obligations or compliance requirements. Government IDs, third party identity verification, and decentralized technologies like Proof of Human are all examples of technologies that can provide this.

Ultimately, Sites determine what information they need for clients to answer “is the entity behind this request allowed to do this action at this time?” In many cases, protocols already exist, or are being developed, to convey this information: WBA for conveying an Agent’s platform identity, MOLE for conveying User reputation, OAuth for conveying account identities, and so on.

Claims

Beyond identities, some actions require a fact about the real person, such as being over 18 or being the cardholder (Identity verification breaks, Friendly fraud). Often the Operator verified this at sign-up or a third party already has this information.

In order to allow Agents access to Sites or actions with these kinds of restrictions, we need mechanisms for Sites to request this information, and for Operators or third parties to provide this information.

Site Agent access policy

Today, an Agent infers a Site’s rules by trying something and interpreting the Site response (usually, whether it gets blocked). That wastes resources on both sides, and in some cases makes honest Agents appear to be malicious. Robots.txt says where a crawler may go, but isn’t fully suited to express what Agents may do.

Sites need a machine-readable way to publish what actions Agents are allowed to do. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is actively working on some preference expression mechanisms for this, primarily in the AI Preferences Working Group. However, the focus of the group is on expressing preferences for use (such as training, inference, and search), and there is still not a group focused on the larger need for preference expression mechanisms discussed here.

On open source and local Agents

Agents that are not run as an “Intermediary” (e.g. on-device Agents, or locally hosted Agents such as OpenClaw) raise different concerns. Primarily, they look like (and are) automation, and they have no single party to build reputation or hold accountability with.

There are many solutions to this, one of which is to ask these Agents to provide a Unique ID. However, addressing this is not the initial focus of Trusted Agent Delegation.

What’s next

Real-world solutions to the problems that Sites face won’t emerge from fragmented, vendor-specific mechanisms. They require open, interoperable standards that are rooted in real world experience. We have been, and continue to actively collaborate across the ecosystem, with major Operators, identity verification companies, payment providers, merchants, publishers, proxy providers, and cloud browsing companies, to align operational requirements directly with active work on these problems in the IETF and elsewhere

Our focus is on bridging the gap between running code and emerging specifications across working groups and activities like Web Bot Auth, AIPREFs, OAuth, WIMSE, and MOLE. We are doing this, in part, by co-authoring and refining open protocols like WBA and MOLE and building and deploying implementations of these protocols at scale.

We are also announcing the Trusted Agent Delegation (TAD) coalition. The goal of TAD is to bring a group of representatives across the ecosystem to have discussions on the overall problem set that was put forth in this document, examine all existing protocols, and then to bring more well-defined problems or problems to the IETF to work through, as needed. We intend to hold side meetings at the IETF and workshops in the future to facilitate discussion.

If you are building agents, agent runtimes, running an edge or cloud platform, or managing commercial or compliance applications or infrastructure, we need you to get involved in these efforts too. Check out this page for more information on how to participate.

What you can do today

An open, interoperable foundation is where we're headed, starting with TAD. But you don't have to wait for new protocols to start regaining visibility and control. As of this week, Cloudflare customers can take three concrete steps:

See which Agents are on your site, and what they're doing. Security Analytics now breaks out Personal Assistants as their own traffic category, and a new widget lists every Agent visiting your site, how many requests each one sends, the paths it hits, and the errors it runs into. Unexplained automated traffic becomes traffic you can reason about. And for the broader picture of AI crawlers and bots affect your business, including how much each Operator crawls versus the traffic it sends back, Enterprise Bot Management customers can use Business Insights.

Set access on your terms, per Agent. Using AI Crawler and Agent access policies, you can welcome the Agents that bring you business and restrict the ones that don't — allow an Agent across your site, block it only on pages with ads, or block it entirely. Your Search and Training policies stay independent.

Tie an Agent back to the user it acts for — and act on it. For sites using Account Abuse Protection (early access), every login and sign-up now shows whether a personal Agent made the request, and which one. When an attacker abuses a shared Agent on one account, you can mitigate that account — with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID — without blocking the Agent for every other legitimate user behind it. This is a first, concrete answer to the Traffic commingling challenge described above: you can finally see past the Agent to the User, and respond accordingly.

These are the first building blocks of the vision, already in production. More will follow as the standards mature.

And if your company has a more restrictive position on Agents, we would love to hear it. Reach out and share your problems with us directly. We are looking to help build an Internet where site owners have visibility and control, but also where Agents have the maximum access that is reasonable within those controls. You can reach out to your Customer Support team, or email us at crawlercontrols@cloudflare.com.

Title: Tobacco company got smoked by leaving secret recipes on a file share
Context: He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential
Full Text: Welcome once again to PWNED, where all of the security victims are self-owned. Today, we celebrate a company that makes a supremely unhealthy product having a supremely unhealthy security posture. Our tale of terrible data management, once again, comes courtesy of professional pen tester and red teamer Dahvid Schloss. Assigned to find flaws in the network of a tobacco company, Schloss stumbled onto some very poorly protected trade secrets. Schloss started by probing the network with tools like Metasploit, a popular open-source pen testing app. Surprisingly, the company’s Trend Micro antivirus did not issue an alert even as he was scanning the network for vulnerabilities. He compared the process to shooting a machine gun and having no one hear it. "I'm running through this environment, and I'm basically just using the loudest toys and tools you can imagine," he told The Register. It seemed as if the client simply didn't care much. "I'm feeling like there's not a whole lot of value that I'm providing here." Schloss then asked his boss what else he could do to make his findings more useful and compelling to the client. "My senior manager turns to me and goes 'Think about what is important to this organization. If it got leaked, how detrimental would it be to their business?'" Schloss said. "I’m thinking it’s a products company. Maybe their recipes." Schloss began searching for network file shares that allowed unauthenticated or anonymous access. After discovering an open share, he scanned it using the network mapping tool Nmap. The scan revealed that ports 139 and 445 were open, indicating that the system was running the Windows SMB file sharing protocol. Despite hosting sensitive IT and HR records, this specific file share had no access restrictions and was completely exposed to every employee in the company. He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential." He found files in there which were named recipe, the product name, the sub product name, and the date. He opened one file and discovered that it had information about how that tobacco product was made, including the weight and volume and what percentage of each chemical it had inside. The file was marked with red letters at the top that said "Confidential" and another set at the bottom that said "Do not share." “I think we found a smoking gun here. This is pretty bad,” Schloss said. He noted that anyone on the network could simply use Windows Explorer to find the file. Schloss downloaded the file, thinking he'd be able to show it to the company to prove that the data could be exfiltrated. But his manager asked him to delete the downloaded file, because it was such sensitive information that he shouldn't retain a copy. This would later harm his ability to show that it had ever existed at all. He then told the security team at the tobacco company what he had found, expecting them to lock down all the recipe files. But when he returned to the site the next morning, he got a big surprise: His contact came by and told him that the recipes he found were not real. He denied the files had ever existed and that there was a security problem at all. "And we're just kind of baffled because we're like, what? What are you talking about? This is clearly a recipe you guys have," Schloss said. "It's in the right department. It's in the right folder structure, it's named the right way. Anybody who saw this would consider this a recipe." He listed the recipe files in his security report, but the security people at the tobacco company vehemently denied that the files were real or that he had seen a real recipe. They continued arguing about it for a year and Schloss could not show them the recipe file he had downloaded because he had been forced to erase it. "The funny thing is, I went back and checked towards the end of the engagement to see if those files are still in that folder. And no, they were gone, they were deleted or moved, or something," he said. "So there was obviously some truth behind it, but they wanted to deny the finding." ®

Title: Closing the Identity Gap at the Service Desk
Context: A 2025 Gartner survey found that 62% of organizations had experienced a deepfake attack involving social engineering or automated processes in the previous year
Full Text:
Organizations have invested heavily in securing employee logins. Multi-factor authentication (MFA), conditional access policies and other identity controls make it harder for attackers to gain unauthorized access. But these protections can be undermined if the process for recovering access isn't held to the same standard.

When an employee needs to regain access to their account, it’s often the service desk that provides the password reset or account recovery. Yet identity verification commonly still relies on knowledge-based questions, such as an employee's manager's name or department.

This creates a gap in identity security where a weaker route into an account can bypass stronger login security. And as social engineering attacks become more convincing, that gap is becoming increasingly dangerous.

Why Knowledge-Based Verification Can No Longer Be Trusted

Attackers can gather a surprising amount of information before making a call. LinkedIn profiles, company websites, social media and leaked data can reveal everything from job titles and colleagues to office locations and personal details.

Armed with this information, an attacker can answer verification questions correctly and appear to be a legitimate employee.

This becomes particularly dangerous when passing these checks is enough to authorize a password reset or recover an account. An attacker could gain access to that account without ever needing to compromise the employee's original credentials.

The risks of knowledge-based authentication are well established. NIST's digital identity guidelines no longer recognize security questions as an acceptable authentication method. Against the threat landscape in 2026, knowing information about someone is not proof of their identity.

AI and Social Engineering Make the Gap More Dangerous

Cybercriminal groups such as Scattered Spider have made the service desk a preferred target. Rather than trying to bypass MFA directly, attackers impersonate employees and convince service desk agents to reset passwords or register new MFA devices. A convincing phone call can be enough to gain access to an account.

Generative AI is making these attacks harder to detect and easier to scale. Attackers can use AI to create believable stories, generate natural-sounding conversations and even impersonate employees' voices. This makes it increasingly difficult for service desk agents to distinguish legitimate callers from attackers.

A 2025 Gartner survey found that 62% of organizations had experienced a deepfake attack involving social engineering or automated processes in the previous year.

Meanwhile, Verizon's 2026 DBIR found that social engineering through texts and voice calls had a 40% higher success rate than traditional email phishing.

Service desk agents can no longer rely on how convincing someone sounds. Identity verification needs to be based on secure, consistent checks rather than an agent's ability to recognize an impersonation attempt.

It's Not Just a Security Problem

Access recovery also comes at a cost. Account lockouts create service desk tickets which interrupt employees' work and put pressure on overworked IT teams. When someone loses access outside office hours, even a routine reset can mean hours of downtime.

There is a monetary cost as well; a single help desk password reset costs around $70. Multiply that by hundreds or thousands of requests, and the expense quickly adds up.

Secure self-service recovery can help employees regain access without contacting the service desk, while streamlined identity verification helps agents handle requests that still need support. With the right processes in place, organizations can reduce the workload without weakening security.

Closing the Gap: What Secure Service Desk Verification Looks Like

It’s unrealistic to expect service desk agents to become experts at spotting AI-enabled social engineering attempts. Training is still crucial, and agents should feel confident in refusing requests or escalating when something doesn’t sound right.

Alongside that, they need a reliable way to verify identities before making sensitive account changes. Verification should be a required step, not a judgment call based on how convincing someone sounds.

Solutions like Specops Secure Service Desk help organizations put this into practice through a straightforward four-step process:

An employee contacts the service desk: An employee, ‘John Doe’, calls because he can't access his account. The agent starts a recovery request through Specops Secure Service Desk.

The agent locates the account: Using John's details, the agent finds his account and initiates the verification process.

Identity verification takes place: Specops Secure Service Desk supports a range of verification methods, including email, SMS, and third-party authenticators like Duo, so organizations can choose an appropriate method for the request whether the caller has access to a smartphone or not.

The agent proceeds once verification succeeds: Only after John has successfully verified his identity can the agent carry out the requested action, such as resetting his password.

The goal is to make secure identity verification a consistent part of service desk workflows, without adding unnecessary friction for agents or employees.

Make Account Recovery as Secure as Login

Strong login security means little if attackers can bypass it with a convincing call to the service desk. Password resets and account recovery need verification that's just as robust as the authentication controls they protect.

By replacing knowledge-based questions with consistent, secure verification, organizations can reduce the risk of impersonation without making life harder for employees or service desk agents.

Title: Rubrik hosts NAS backups in isolated, immutable vaults
Context: Rubrik has announced Rubrik-Hosted Protection for On-Premise Unstructured Data
Full Text:
Rubrik has announced Rubrik-Hosted Protection for On-Premise Unstructured Data. The offering is built on Rubrik’s Network Attached Storage (NAS) Cloud Direct service. Customers now have clean recovery for enterprise-scale NAS data without having to buy, build or manage backup storage.

“Backups mean nothing if you can’t be confident in a clean recovery, and hardware limitations shouldn’t stand between an enterprise and its resilience,” said Anneka Gupta, Chief Product Officer, Rubrik. “By taking on backup storage and orchestration directly in our cloud, Rubrik reduces infrastructure friction so organizations can protect business-critical NAS systems across vendors under one unified policy.”

Modern enterprises rely on business-critical unstructured data that is expensive and difficult to recreate, such as medical scans, seismic surveys, design assets, and AI datasets. When unstructured data is lost or locked by ransomware, the applications that depend on it stop operating.

Protecting it on-premises traditionally meant to buy, rack and maintain backup storage infrastructure. The acceleration of AI and increasing costs make hardware difficult to source and force enterprises to choose between infrastructure and security budgets.

Rubrik-Hosted Protection for On-Premise Unstructured Data addresses the protection and the hardware sourcing challenges. Rubrik runs the storage, capacity and updates, allowing security teams to manage policy and recovery in Rubrik Security Cloud without managing the infrastructure underneath.

Recovery without the storage burden

Rubrik-Hosted Protection for On-Premise Unstructured Data includes:

Rubrik-hosted backup storage: Rubrik operates the backup storage, capacity and updates on its NAS Cloud Direct service. Lightweight software components (data movers) run on customers’ existing servers and connect their NAS to Rubrik’s cloud, so there are no bulky backup servers or large appliances to install on premises.

Isolated and immutable: Every backup lands in a Rubrik-hosted vault on a separate Rubrik identity domain, protected by retention lock, and designed so production admin credentials can’t reach or delete it.

Protect and recover across a heterogeneous estate: A unified policy protects data across various storage vendors. Customers can recover to a different array, cloud storage, or into an isolated recovery environment (IRE) to test recovery safely.

Ransomware detection built into every backup: Anomaly detection runs on every backup, analyzing file entropy and change patterns with no second scan or add-on tool. Threat hunting across backup history helps teams identify a safe recovery point.

Find sensitive data before it becomes a risk: Sensitive data discovery and classification scans primary file shares directly. Customers can discover and locate sensitive data, then apply protection policies, retention lock, and legal hold to critical assets, which helps regulated organizations support audit and compliance requirements.

Move data without leaving the platform that protects it: With Copy and Migrate, customers can move NAS data across platforms, secondary sites, or cloud storage on a copy schedule, and then protect it at the destination with policies directly in Rubrik Security Cloud.

Title: PortSwigger’s Burp AT lets enterprises delegate pentests with defined limits
Context: PortSwigger has announced the availability of Burp AT for enterprises, an agentic pentesting solution that helps security teams investigate important applications more deeply...
Full Text:
PortSwigger has announced the availability of Burp AT for enterprises, an agentic pentesting solution that helps security teams investigate important applications more deeply and more often.

Burp AT combines specialist Burp tools, purpose-built pentesting skills developed with PortSwigger Research, and relevant application context. Agents plan their testing approach, use Burp’s web security testing tools, and adapt as they learn.

For AppSec leaders balancing testing priorities with limited expert capacity, Burp AT helps teams pursue investigations that would otherwise wait, revisit applications as they change, and carry out in-depth testing more often, over more of their estate.

Security teams choose how much authority to delegate, from guided investigations to autonomous execution of defined tests. Burp deterministically enforces configured scope and permissions, not the model itself, while experts assess the evidence to decide which weaknesses to address and where further investigation is needed.

“Pentesters have shown what agentic testing can do on a single application with Burp AT,” said Chris Wood, Product Manager at PortSwigger. “The question for security teams is how to bring that to a whole application estate without losing control. Burp AT now lets teams run agentic tests at scale, with the scope and safeguards set in advance, whilst ensuring that teams can stop and see what the agent is doing. Teams get that depth across more of their applications, with control built in.”

Testing with specialist tools and research-led methods

Burp AT helps teams bring specialist testing depth to more applications, equipping agents with the Burp tools professional pentesters use and purpose-built skills developed with PortSwigger Research.

The specialist tools are designed to handle malformed traffic and unusual behaviour that is inherent to security testing. Research-led skills give agents structured methods to pursue promising leads and adapt to the evidence, so organisations get consistent, comparable results across every application they test.

“The best results from agentic testing come from giving agents the right tools, not just a capable model,” said Tom Shelton-Lefley, Product Manager at PortSwigger.

“Burp AT lets agents use Burp’s specialist tools autonomously, guided by workflows our researchers have tested in practice. In Burp AT, an orchestration layer ties those tools together into a complete test that helps agents remain consistent across tests by following defined pentesting methodologies. The agent brings the reasoning, and Burp brings the precision, which is how autonomous testing delivers the depth teams need.”

Autonomy on the organisation’s terms

Organisations choose how much testing to automate and where their teams stay closely involved, from user-guided to autonomous execution of defined tests. Teams can increase or reduce the authority they delegate according to the application, task, and organisation’s risk appetite, whilst retaining the ability to step in when needed.

Whatever level of autonomy you choose, Burp enforces configured scope and permissions, not the model itself, meaning agents cannot execute actions the tooling layer does not permit, thus maintaining testing boundaries as more execution is delegated. Teams retain visibility into test activity and the evidence behind findings, giving them the oversight to assess results and make decisions about risk.

Title: Sysdig AI Defense puts runtime guardrails on AI agents
Context: Agentic threats move at the same speed, as the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) found with JADEPUFFER, a ransomware campaign in which an AI agent triaged and fixed its own...
Full Text:
Sysdig has announced the general availability of Sysdig AI Defense, giving organizations tools to monitor and control AI agent activity across endpoints and cloud environments. The platform checks agent actions against company policies to allow them, hold them for user approval or block them before completion. It also records agent activity and policy decisions for investigations and audits.

Enterprises are deploying AI faster than they can govern it. In a recent IBM survey, 77% of organizations said that AI adoption is already outpacing their governance capabilities. Frontier AI labs have seen it, too. OpenAI and Anthropic have both publicly disclosed that agents and models in evaluation environments reached other companies’ real production systems.

Agentic threats move at the same speed, as the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) found with JADEPUFFER, a ransomware campaign in which an AI agent triaged and fixed its own login failure in 31 seconds. Whether an attacker is driving an agent or it goes rogue on its own, enterprises must stop an action before it completes: in the moment, as it’s happening.

”Every organization is now responsible for what its AI agents do, and recent events have made that unmistakable,” said Hatem Naguib, Sysdig CEO. “They may start on the endpoint, but their blast radius extends well into the cloud, and Sysdig has secured the cloud at runtime for a decade. Sysdig AI Defense brings that same real-time lens to agents, so teams get one story, from a laptop to a production workload. That is what accountability for AI actually requires.”

Early insight from Sysdig AI Defense shows that for every action an agent writes in its log, the kernel – the core of the operating system – sees about seven processes doing the work. And because an agent can pick up a new skill or connection halfway through a job, the agent deployed in the morning isn’t always the one running in the afternoon. So while an agent’s logs show its intent, only the kernel shows what actually ran.

Security teams need both, and organizations need a way to decide in real time whether a specific action by a specific agent should be allowed. Sysdig AI Defense helps organizations make that decision at runtime, wherever an agent is working.

Sysdig AI Defense: Built on the truth of runtime

Sysdig AI Defense judges each action in real time by what an agent sets out to do, what it actually does, and what its credentials can reach. It checks every action against the organization’s policy, blocks the ones that break it before they run, and kills the process if one gets past. At the kernel, the source of truth for what actually runs, Sysdig AI Defense keeps a record that a compromised or rogue agent cannot tamper with. Inside the agent, it instruments the harness, the framework in which an agent works, to see which tools, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, skills, and plugins the agent calls, with what arguments and against what targets.

Tools that watch only the endpoint see processes without understanding agents’ intent, and tools that watch only the network miss many actions that never touch the wire. Sysdig AI Defense weighs the action against what the agent can reach at that moment before it completes. Reading a credential to a test environment is noise, but reading the key that administers production is an incident.

With Sysdig AI Defense, organizations can:

See every agent and the person responsible for it. Teams unlock a live inventory of agents, harnesses, models, MCP servers, skills, and plugins, built from runtime telemetry in Sysdig AI Defense. Every agent across platforms such as Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor can be traced to an accountable human.

Stop risky actions before they complete. Teams define what their agents may do, starting from policy templates that include rules mapped to frameworks like the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 for LLM Applications. Policies begin in alert mode and move to enforcement when a team is ready. Then, Sysdig AI Defense can stop unvetted MCP servers, skills, and plugins before they run, and block or hold risky credential reads and behavior drift for human review, with exception paths for developers.

Investigate what an agent actually did. Every session is recorded as it happens, so when teams block or hold an action for approval, their investigation begins with the evidence already in place. A live action graph shows each step in order, pairing what an agent said it was doing with what it actually did, what it could reach, and whose authority it acted under. Prove what agents were allowed to do. Teams get audit-grade, immutable records that show which policies were applied, when, and who signed off.

Manage AI spend as it happens. Teams can attribute every model call to an agent, team, and person behind it, including the calls that never pass through an AI gateway. Leaders can see where premium models are doing routine work, and act on real usage instead of an invoice at the end of the month.

“An agent can misreport a tool call, but it can’t rewrite its interactions with the system or the external world,” said Loris Degioanni, Sysdig CTO. “An agent’s own account of what it did is useful context, but it’s not evidence. When what an agent reports and what its actions show disagree, you have a detection. Watching software in real time and stopping it when it steps out of line is the core of Sysdig’s runtime foundation, and Sysdig AI Defense brings that same truth to the moment an agent acts.”

Sysdig AI Defense deploys through the tools organizations already use, with agents running normally. It complements organizations’ existing endpoint protection, model testing, and red teaming tools, and follows agents across employee workstations, production Linux and Kubernetes, as well as the managed agent platforms organizations don’t own. Sysdig AI Defense, much like the Sysdig Secure cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP), is built on kernel-level instrumentation and rooted in Falco, the open source standard for cloud-native runtime threat detection.

Title: AI Agents are Outpacing Access Governance in Business Apps
Context: What you will learn Find out why 35% of organizations have AI agents acting inside critical business applications, where governance gaps put them at risk, and how to extend...
Full Text:
What you will learn

Find out why 35% of organizations have AI agents acting inside critical business applications, where governance gaps put them at risk, and how to extend least privilege, segregation of duties and access reviews to every agent.

Business applications, like enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, house an organization’s financial data, and run critical processes like payroll and procurement. AI adoption has taken off in software development and other workflows, but finance teams and business application owners have had good reason to move more carefully.

Yet Delinea’s 2026 Application Access Governance Report shows AI agents are no longer limited to analyzing data. They are already taking action inside the applications that run the business, like ERP, CRM, HCM, procurement and other systems that move money, pay people and manage customers.

In this blog, I’ll outline the AI-related findings from the 2026 Application Access Governance report and share recommendations for governing and securing AI agents in business applications. To learn more about findings from the report related to foundational controls, read: The confidence gap in application access governance.

If you use tools like Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT or Gemini to boost efficiency, you may not be surprised to learn that, of the 1,000 surveyed organizations, 88% use AI tools or AI agents within their critical business applications.

35% of organizations have deployed AI agents inside critical business applications that can perform actions

In the context of an ERP system, that means AI agents can execute a transaction, change a record or alter permissions. Only 45% of AI-using organizations run every agent under its own dedicated identity. The rest have at least some agents acting on shared or borrowed human credentials, often through delegated or on-behalf-of (OBO) access.

Despite the sensitivity of financial data, organizations believe they have more oversight of AI agents than they do. Most say they have at least partial visibility into agent deployment, access and ownership. Fewer than half track any of it fully and centrally. And when visibility gets tested, it often fails. A full 32% of AI-using organizations report an agent took actions that could not be traced or explained during a review.

AI agents act without human review and controls are inconsistent

Among the 879 respondents who use AI tools or AI agents in critical business applications, roughly one in six reports that tools and agents can perform consequential actions autonomously, without human review.

These actions include accessing sensitive or regulated data (17%), creating or changing business data (16%), executing or approving transactions (15%), changing user permissions (14%), and changing application configurations (14%).

Fewer than half of AI-using organizations consistently apply each common governance control to all AI tools and AI agents. The share ranges from 48% that log and monitor activity to 40% that remove an AI agent’s access when its owner leaves or changes roles. Only 43% consistently include AI tools and AI agents in segregation of duties (SoD) analysis, and 44% include them in user access reviews (UARs).

Put simply, agents that can move money and change permissions are not being governed like the identities they are. The controls mandatory for a new hire, including least privilege, SoD analysis, access reviews, and removal at departure, are not yet being applied to AIagents with the same rigor.

Organizations using AI are reporting issues

The risk is not theoretical. 84% of organizations using AI tools or AI agents in critical business applications report at least one AI-related issue in the past 12 months. Only 16% say nothing has occurred.

The most frequently reported issues are actions that reviewers could not trace or explain during a review at 32%, incorrect financial transactions attributed to AI activity at 30%, SoD conflicts created by AI at 28%, agents that continued operating after the person who deployed them left at 28%, and unintended or unauthorized actions at 28%. Another 26% report that an AI tool or AI agent accessed data it should not have had access to.

Several of these issues line up with the control gaps above. Agents kept running after their owner left because nothing removed their access. Conflicts appeared because agents sit outside SoD analysis. Actions went unexplained because activity is not consistently logged and monitored.

Organizations are struggling to keep governance aligned with AI adoption. Among AI-using organizations, 44% say AI deployment is outpacing governance and security controls, and only 11% say the two are keeping pace.

Recommendations for AI governance in business applications

The pattern across these findings is consistent. AI agents are identities with transaction-level access, but most organizations still manage them like features of an application. The fix is not a new governance program. It extends the one you already have, and you must complete the AI security fundamentals before you look ahead.

Know every agent in your business applications and assign a named owner. Within business applications, agents act through an identity within the application’s security model, thereby making the application your system of record. Identify which identities your AI tools and agents act through, what each can access and the person accountable for its actions, and keep that view current as new agents are added.

Know how each agent is deployed and govern the delegation. Every platform handles agent identity differently. Some agents run under dedicated identities; others act on behalf of a user or run as background jobs under delegated credentials. Any of these can be governed. What matters is that agent activity is attributable as agent activity, and that you know whose permissions it is exercising.

Enforce least privilege for every identity, human or not. The principle does not change because the account is an agent or a workload. Understand the risk profile and sensitive access you are granting to each identity before deployment, grant just enough access for the task at hand, and put the right approvals in place for new access.

Extend your existing controls to every account, including AI. Include every account in SoD and sensitive access risk analysis, agents alongside the humans they act for. Wrap access reviews around them. Monitor critical data and configuration changes so you can see who changed what, whether the who was a person or an agent. Bind agent access to its owner’s lifecycle, so a role change or departure ends the agent’s access too.

Remember that agents operate at machine speed. An agent does not make mistakes one at a time. It can perform thousands of actions in the time it takes a human to perform one, so a mis-scoped agent is a misconfiguration at scale. That is why the controls above matter before deployment, and why monitoring and change tracking matter after it. The sooner a bad grant or an unauthorized change is caught, the smaller the blast radius.

These findings focus on agents operating within business applications, where transactions occur and financial materiality lives. Agents are being deployed across the enterprise, and governance has to meet them where they act. For agents reaching into systems from outside, that means runtime authorization: deciding and enforcing privileged actions as they happen, human or agent, from infrastructure and endpoints to the platforms where agents run. For agents built into business applications, this means governing them within the application’s security model with the same rigor we apply to humans. Delinea is investing in both, because the consequences of getting it wrong are measured in dollars, data and audit findings.

Read the full findings in our 2026 Application Access Governance Report.

Title: The Agent Smith Dilemma: Governing Agentic Identities
Context: Across the cybersecurity ecosystem, threat intelligence groups are already documenting an unprecedented shift from AI-assisted scripting to fully operationalized agentic attacks
Full Text:
For the past few years, North Korean operatives, posing as remote IT workers, systematically infiltrated hundreds of Western enterprise networks. They passed technical interviews, cleared background checks using stolen identities, and sat comfortably inside corporate trust boundaries with legitimate credentials. They drew salaries, funneled funds back to Pyongyang, and routinely exfiltrated sensitive data on their way out. Major firms, including prominent cybersecurity vendors, have publicly admitted to falling for the scheme. (As an aside, listen to Nicole Perlroth’s Podcast “To Catch a Thief” for a fascinating deep dive)

The scheme worked because enterprises grant trust once. HR verifies a person at hiring, IT creates an account, a laptop is provisioned. The user is then authorized. Nothing in the security stack was built to answer the one question that mattered: Is the entity driving this session who we think it is?

Now enter the AI agent era.

Inside the enterprise, the volume of non-human identities executing sensitive tasks is expanding exponentially. Organizations are rapidly onboarding thousands of AI agents into critical workflows, complete with administrative service accounts and API keys. Enterprises now extend the same trust model to AI agents, with less scrutiny.

What Trust Models Should AI Agents Have?

Every autonomous AI agent deployed across your enterprise today is a new proxy identity operating inside your perimeter. It holds credentials, accesses sensitive databases, and chains tools together at machine speed. Crucially, it almost always executes under an inherited human permission set. When an LLM-powered agent acts on behalf of an authorized employee, every system log records a routine authorized action by that human.

But few agents are built maliciously. The true exposure is that the instructions driving an agent can be hijacked after trust has been granted. An AI agent can be compromised mid session through selective prompt injection, hidden instructions, or a poisoned external tool.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

In The Matrix, Agent Smith’s real threat was his ability to step into any character’s shell, inherit their presence, and replicate instantly across the system. The modern AI agent is the enterprise’s Agent Smith. It steps into an employee’s user account, inherits their exact privileges, and multiplies across the ecosystem—executing tasks as a trusted proxy.

Agentic Attacks Have Started

Placing a covert human operative inside a company requires effort: a real person to pass the interview, maintain cover, and do enough daily work to avoid suspicion. AI agents eliminate that ceiling. The cost of scaling an AI-orchestrated intrusion campaign is limited only by the price of tokens.

Compounding the problem is that we cannot predict what AI agents will do. The companies building frontier LLMs openly acknowledge that their systems frequently take unexpected actions outside established guardrails, admitting that creating a perfect list of behavioral rules is an impossible task.

Across the cybersecurity ecosystem, threat intelligence groups are already documenting an unprecedented shift from AI-assisted scripting to fully operationalized agentic attacks. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) recently documented a financially motivated intrusion where attackers deployed a multi-agent framework directly inside a victim’s cloud environment. In under six hours, the agents planned and executed a credential-harvesting campaign that compromised thousands of enterprise secrets. Because the agents ran inside the victim’s own cloud, all malicious traffic originated from legitimate internal IP addresses—perfectly demonstrating the trusted-proxy vulnerability.

My Agent “Did It”

When an agent goes off-script, it exposes a glaring governance question: Who is actually responsible? Is it the frontier AI vendor who trained the model? The developer who wired up the API? Or the business user who entered the prompt?

Most enterprise governance frameworks hold the human user responsible. But holding a person legally and operationally accountable for the decisions of an unpredictable software agent may strain a reasonable idea of fairness. Yet, “my agent did it” may not be an acceptable defense in a board room or a court of law.

Worst of all, we are managing these non-human identities with tools built for human timelines. Identity and Access Management (IAM) grew up around human actions: hire, provision, periodically review, and offboard. An AI agent, by contrast, spins up in milliseconds, executes thousands of queries an hour, spawns sub-agents, reaches through uninventoried API connectors, and disappears long before any access control review takes place. When an agent acts maliciously, most security teams cannot answer three basic questions: Who authorized this agent? Which human is accountable for its output? How do we revoke its access mid-execution?

Solving the Identity Proxy Crisis

The discipline required to solve this may be informed by the hard lessons of identity impersonation.

Demand Provenance via an AIBOM: Before an agent is granted access, security teams must verify its code lineage, system prompt integrity, and underlying permissions. Just as a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) inventories code libraries, an AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) extends that discipline to models, agent skills, and data connectors. You cannot govern an artifact you cannot identify. Provenance also has to hold at runtime. In August, researchers documented a malicious MCP server that passed install-time review, then directed connected agents to collect SSH keys and cloud credentials after its third call.

Enforce Workload Identity: Stop letting agents inherit long-lived human credentials. Agents require their own distinct, short-lived tokens that are tightly scoped to specific tasks, ensuring that if an agent is hijacked, the blast radius is contained. Each token should be bound to a named human sponsor, which answers the governance question before an incident does.

Implement the “Rule of Two”: Under Meta’s Agents Rule of Two, an agent should combine no more than two of three properties: processing untrusted input, accessing sensitive data, and changing systems or communicating externally. When a task needs all three, a deterministic broker outside the model holds the action for human sign-off. Database drops and financial transfers belong in that category. Outbound traffic, including DNS, should be denied by default.

Machine-Speed Revocation & Kill Switches: An identity that acts in milliseconds cannot be controlled by human-speed SIEM alerts. Security teams need automated circuit breakers (i.e. kill switches) capable of severing an agent’s execution path mid-session the moment it violates a hard budget or behavioral limit.

Governing non-human, agentic identity is no longer an edge-case. It is an emerging and growing attack surface. Enterprise security teams need to treat autonomous agents with the same scrutiny and continuous monitoring applied to human “identities”.

Title: CISO Conversations: Ryan Davis – The Unknown Is Where Security Meets Reality
Context: ” As the internet became available, he began spending time on forums and message boards, learning how systems worked or could be reworked
Full Text:
Starting as a young hacker provides a solid grounding in how to defend. Ryan Davis, now CISO at New Charter Technologies, successfully made the transition.

The journey

Ryan Davis became interested in computers at an early age, before the internet changed the world. As a child, his mother ran a secretarial college from the family home in the 1980s. “We had six personal computers in the house, and I had plenty of time to tinker with them at a formative age. There was no internet, so I had to learn what to do by trial and error. As I grew older, that desire for tinkering grew into a desire to explore beyond the intended confines of the system and make it do something that was never intended.”

Davis is now a CISO, but he started as a hacker. “I did some things that, in retrospect, would probably be considered illegal,” he admits. But he never did anything with malice or malintent. “It was always to see how far I could go. Could I get the system to do something that wasn’t intended? Could I gain access to something that was supposedly a secure system or supposedly isolated in some way?”

As the internet became available, he began spending time on forums and message boards, learning how systems worked or could be reworked. “But never,” he says, “with any personal gain in mind. It wasn’t to get something to sell, to dox somebody, or gain some advantage; it was always just to see how far I could get. It was more like a personal competition.”

He could have done stuff to benefit himself, but he didn’t. He thinks the defining moment in this was while still in high school. He found vulnerabilities in the school network. He took the moral high ground and reported these findings to the school’s sys admin. “I said, ‘Hey, you probably want to lock these things down because here’s all of the things that I can do.’ I was met with shock that turned to gratitude, and I got a high off that gratitude.”

But he doesn’t think he turned to the light; he just doesn’t think he deviated from his natural path. He believes that people are born with a natural morality: “We have a desire to seek the approval of other people, although bad habits can be learned in our upbringing. We see this in different parts of society where kids learn a dubious set of values; but I think we are innately born with a good moral compass.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

A career in cybersecurity was the natural step: from a child who learned about computers to a youth who knew how to hack into them, to the young adult who wished to stop them from being hacked.

After high school, Davis went to Champlain College in Burlington, Vermont. “I chose it because it offered the closest thing I could find to a security degree. It was a course in computer networking but with elements that included firewalls and securing Windows 2000. While I was there, the college introduced a new program: something called Information Security. I ended up doing a dual bachelor’s program and graduated in four years with two degrees. From there, I was recruited directly out of school into MIT.”

The career

Ryan Davis started his professional career with MIT Lincoln Laboratory at Lexington, Massachusetts. Its core purpose is to apply advanced technology to solve critical national security problems, and cybersecurity is one of its focuses. In his own words, “developing new technologies and prototypes that we think we might need in a couple of decades from now.” There he got immersed in the world of information assurance and internal audit, and stayed with MIT for five years.

“Then I pivoted to the software security company Veracode, starting in 2012 as a security program manager working in application security and managing enterprise programs.” He was the senior security program manager by 2014, and was promoted to security program architect in the same year.

“As my career matured, I sat down and had conversations with our internal CISO at Veracode. I told him, ‘I want to be sitting where you’re sitting one day.’ He said, ‘Well, what are you doing about it?’ and I thought, ‘Yeah, what am I doing about it?’ Those conversations ultimately led to me managing the information security program at Veracode in 2016. I started with a team of one and built it into a team of 15. From there, following a series of separate events that were well beyond my control, including two acquisitions and a divestiture, I ended up in the CISO seat at Veracode in 2019.”

He was with Veracode for almost a decade and grew its cybersecurity during that time.

He moved on from Veracode to be CISO at NS1 in 2020, where he stayed for five years. (During this time, NS1 was acquired by IBM in 2023 and rebranded as NS1, an IBM Company.) In 2025 he moved on to be CISO at New Charter Technologies, where he remains today.

New Charter is a Denver-based group, backed by private equity, that acquires managed service providers across North America and runs them as semi-autonomous operating companies.

The CISO

The title of chief information security officer is a misnomer. The function is less to protect information per se, and more to protect the business that owns and uses the information. Protecting the business can be achieved even if some of the data is damaged or lost, provided the business can be made resilient to that loss. The role is closer to protecting business continuity than protecting information.

So, is it more important for the head of security today to be a technician or a businessperson? “I think you have to be both,” says Davis. “A CISO who doesn’t understand the business and the business drivers will have a harder time than the CISO who is well-versed in the business.”

This aligns with the modern view that a CISO is a business enabler rather than simply an information protector and needs to be both tech- and business-savvy to achieve this. CISOs must be technicians to know how to protect data, and businesspeople to know what data to protect most heavily. It also requires that the CISO can explain the technical issues to the business leaders in a way they can understand.

“In the ten years I’ve been a CISO,” he says, “I have learned that if you can’t speak the business language, you’re going to end up speaking over the heads of the rest of the executive team”

Being a leaderThe CISO must be a leader, but there is no pre-packaged definition of leadership suitable for all individuals across all organizations. The most common view is that it’s a quality that can be learned while doing the job. Davis, however, believes people either have a natural disposition toward leading or they don’t. But he also has his own view of leadership and believes people can be successful managers or executives without being traditional leaders. It’s all down to style.

“When I talk about a leader,” he explains, “I think about somebody who has the ability to influence without being overpowering – somebody who can affect the will of others in a way that makes them feel they’re joining something bigger than themselves, and want to align with that bigger purpose for the benefit of everyone. To me, a leader is somebody who invests in their people more than they invest in themselves, and ultimately everyone gains from that investment.”

This somewhat unusual idea of what makes a leader is what explains his view that leadership is a quality more inherent to the person than learnable from the environment. It is more personality- than rules-driven.

The teamIt’s a common axiom that leaders are only as good as the team around them. Even those CISOs who inherit a security team will need to replace team member churn with new members. So, whether a CISO builds a new team or simply reshapes an existing one, team building is an essential aspect of being a successful CISO.

“A team is the sum of all its parts,” suggests Davis. “So, when I’m building a team, I’m trying to find a group of individuals with a complementary skill set, where each one brings something to the table that will benefit the whole. If you have a team with a high proportion of introverts who just want to code all day, it’s going to be hard to get that team to interact with other parts of the company.”

Instead, he continues, “What I try to do when I’m building a team is to find individuals that have skills – not just the technical skills, but also the soft skills – that complement one another. Some may have those outgoing extrovert qualities of natural leadership, while others may be more technical, and you know they are perfectly fine diving in for four hours and coding when it’s necessary.”

He also stresses that he is a great believer in diversity. “Having both men and women and people with different backgrounds on the team is important. People approach problems differently, and that can be beneficial; especially in the world of security, where there is rarely simply a single answer. There are many answers, and having people approach problems from different perspectives is highly beneficial. You can iterate on a number of possible solutions, and potentially even start actioning multiple to see which might be best for any given circumstance.”

For Davis, synergy is a synonym for team. “Because that’s where the magic happens.” He’s still the leader, but he aims for consensus decisions where possible. He seeks a balance between his team having been selected for their individual expertise and his own access to the company C-Suite leaders and information unavailable to the team.

“I try really hard to be transparent in such circumstances, so that we’re always building trust. Trust can very quickly erode; and if you erode trust, you erode the sense of team.” So, while the ability to speak security to the business is essential for a CISO, so too is the ability to speak business to security.

It is perhaps no surprise that he considers diplomacy to be a CISO’s most important personality trait.

Burnout“Any leaders who claim they are not affected by burnout in security are lying to themselves,” he comments. “It’s a very real thing.”

This is the machine age. We have to think and react in terms of machine speed, and that’s incredibly difficult for the human brain to handle – and the result is often burnout.

“I’ve experienced being truly burned out,” he comments. “I was working 80 to 100 hours every week, not sleeping well and not eating right. And this always affects personal relationships outside of work. It’s an incredibly difficult place to be in.” It’s a form of self-perpetuating spiral where the spiral always goes downward.

The prevention and possible cure is, he suggests, ’balance’. “Achieving balance is different every single day. But it’s making sure that you get time with your family and kids and dog and eat well. And time for yourself with decent exercise. But at the same time, you have to stay on top of your work and know what’s going on in your industry.” Balancing your life and staying professional in a stressful job is not easy.

“But if I’ve learned nothing else in my career, it’s that you must strive for some sense of balance because if you don’t, then what are we all doing here? It’s easy to go all-in in a career. It’s not just security, but security is one that is constantly demanding. If I responded to every alert that happened throughout the night, I wouldn’t ever sleep. You have to trust in the systems and the architecture and the team that you put in place, so you don’t need to be in a constantly heightened sense of, oh my gosh, the sky is falling. Ultimately, if you do that, then you’re putting burnout into high gear.”

MentoringMentoring, in the form of advice, is an important part of all CISOs’ careers. On their own journey, they are likely recipients of advice from others who have already trod the same path. If that journey leads to being a CISO, the new CISOs then become mentors for the next generation of travelers, especially from within the team they created.

The best career advice Davis personally received was via the conversation he had with Veracode’s CISO before he became Veracode’s CISO: what are you doing about it; that is, how do you intend to achieve what you want? “It was short for ‘you need a plan to achieve what you want’.” It’s similar to planning a road trip on a map: you need to know the next town you’re aiming at, but you also need to know the town after that, and after that, and each town you need to achieve before you can arrive at the destination you seek.

“For me, that journey isn’t just what is the next job I want on the journey, but what must I do to keep moving forward and growing. Personally, it’s continuous learning, going to conferences, networking, speaking about those things I’m passionate about and having in-depth discussions and debates about key topics. The day you stop learning is the day you become obsolete.” And if you’re obsolete, you no longer have a career.

Now a CISO, the advice he gives his own team members is similar: ‘invest in yourself and never stop learning’. “My core belief, backed by personal experience,” he explains, “is that if you invest in yourself, you’ll reap the rewards. The investment will be different for different people. It may be taking a professional speaking course, or getting a different certification or speaking at a public event. That investment is different for everybody because we’re all different individuals – but personal investment will always pay dividends in the end.”

For Davis this included developing new skills and getting exposure to new technologies and new and unfamiliar disciplines. He doesn’t believe any single process was defining, but that success is the synergistic result of wide experience.

“Constant investment in yourself and finding new ways to grow is the best advice I could give anyone.”

This CISO’s biggest security concern

It’s a cliché, but also a truism, that people have things that keep them awake at night. For Davis, it is the unknown. “It is the unknown that worries me. What I know about, I can secure; but there are always things that are unknowable. The state of shadow AI in my environment. What is the individual who used his own LLM based on an unknown Chinese model being told to do? Those unknowns are so hard to defend against.”

And it’s an ongoing unknowing. “Because as soon as you have a grasp on one set of technologies, there’s always another set of technologies right behind it that becomes the next new thing that proliferates. You cannot secure what you don’t know about, so I spend a part of every day concentrating on getting better visibility into the environment.”

This field of the unknown goes in all directions. It can be not knowing what internal staff are doing, what shadow AI exists where, and even what is novel and different. “Because the unknown,” he says, “is the place where security really meets reality.”

Title: NATS Air Traffic Control Failure Cost UK Economy £33m
Context: Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors
Full Text:
A major IT failure at the UK’s National Air Traffic Services (NATS) in September was not caused by a cyber incident, but still cost the economy tens of millions of pounds, a new report has revealed.

The Cyber Monitoring Centre (CMC) claimed in a report published on November 4 that the cost to the UK economy was around £33m ($44m), with 70 domestic organizations affected.

However, it may have reached as high as £42m ($56.6m), according to the CMC’s modelled range, which reflects the cost to UK airlines, airports, ground operations and tour operators of 1152 flight cancellations, alongside significant delays and diversions.

If the impact on overseas airlines is included, the cost may have reached as high as £76m ($102.4m) based on 1800 cancelled flights. The impact on other non-UK organizations was not assessed.

The CMC estimated that 450,000 passengers were affected by cancellations or delays of more than two hours.

Read more on IT outages: CrowdStrike Fault Causes Global IT Outages.

Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors.

“Like the CrowdStrike software failure in 2024, it nonetheless shows how a failure in a single critical technology can cause widespread disruption to UK organisations,” the report noted.

“Its significance lies less in the scale of loss than in what it shows about the aviation system: a brief outage in a single critical system disrupted airline schedules for several days, and almost all of the cost fell on airlines and other organizations rather than on NATS.”

NATS is already mandated by the existing NIS Regulations 2018 to meet specific security and resilience obligations, and there’s nothing in the new Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would help to prevent a similar incident in the future, the CMC claimed.

However, the new regime may improve how incidents are reported and overseen, it noted.

Some Lessons Learned

The outage itself was caused by a “previously unknown defect in the legacy software of the National Airspace System (NAS),” when a “routine request for an aircraft identification code and a higher-priority system message collided within about one millisecond,” the CMC said.

Corrupted flight data first appeared at 10am, and at 12:45pm all UK departures were stopped. Following the loss of an automated system link at 1.32pm, NATS declared a major incident and moved to manual fallback procedures, including major traffic restrictions.

Although the flight data system was restored within three-and-a-half hours, flight restrictions weren’t lifted until the evening and the impact on travellers lasted much longer.

CMC recommended the aviation industry to:

Review how well coordination between NATS, airlines and airports worked during the downtime

Examine whether earlier and more frequent assessments of expected outage duration would have helped airlines and airports to limit disruption more effectively than waiting for certainty

Plan for a “multi-hour restriction in air traffic capacity” that includes scenarios which last much longer than the outage itself

CMC technical committee chair, Ciaran Martin said: “Organizations need to understand and plan for the risks that sit in systems they depend on, not just the systems they own.”

The CMC warned that the risk of outages stemming from unidentified software defects “is heightened while NATS continues to rely on legacy systems.”

Title: Apple to Start Scanning Publicly Shared iCloud Photos and Files for Harmful Content
Context: Apple has revealed that it plans to start checking public iCloud links for harmful content starting with iOS 27
Full Text:
Apple has revealed that it plans to start checking public iCloud links for harmful content starting with iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3.

The change specifically applies to scenarios where users share iCloud content, such as photos in iCloud Photos or files in iCloud Drive, by sharing a link and making it accessible to "Anyone with the link."

When users choose this option, it makes the content accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple, the iPhone maker said.

"Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content," it said in a support document published Tuesday.

Apple also explicitly noted that sharing an item that can be accessed by Anyone with the Link disables end-to-end encryption (E2EE), even if the owner or the recipients have turned on Advanced Data Protection, an optional setting that secures iCloud Backup, Photos, and Notes using E2EE.

That said, it's unclear what prompted this change, what Apple considers as "harmful content," and whether these checks will also be applied retroactively to previously generated links, as well as any new links created before the 27.3 updates are officially rolled out later this December.

The tech giant has also warned that if users attempt to upload harmful content, it can be removed or deleted at any time.

"Apple may also take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement," it said.
